extraction.description: A group of publicly released datasets for visual question answering that enable VQA systems to be trained and evaluated. The paper lists the main datasets as DAQUAR, COCO-QA, The VQA Dataset, FM-IQA, Visual7W, and Visual Genome.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The section describes multiple VQA datasets collected in different ways: DAQUAR uses QA pairs based on images from the NYU-DepthV2 dataset; COCO-QA generates QA pairs automatically from COCO image captions using an NLP algorithm; FM-IQA is based on COCO and contains human-generated questions and answers; Visual Genome used two human-annotation modes, free-form question asking and region-specific prompting based on descriptive bounding boxes; SHAPES consists of synthetic shape images with a fixed set of questions asked about each image.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw/source data included images from NYU-DepthV2, COCO image captions, COCO images, YFCC100M and COCO images for Visual Genome, descriptive bounding-box annotations for region-specific prompting, and synthetic images of shapes.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: For COCO-QA, question-answer pairs were automatically generated from COCO image captions using an NLP algorithm. For The VQA Dataset, annotators generated answers per question; FM-IQA proposed human judges to rate multi-word answers on a 3-point scale.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Annotation quality/diversity was analyzed via inter-human agreement on COCO-VQA, reported as 83.3%, with especially poor agreement for 'Why' questions; the text also discusses consensus-based use of multiple human answers.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: DAQUAR-consensus collected an average of 5 human answers per question; The VQA Dataset collected 10 answers per question.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: An NLP algorithm was used to automatically derive COCO-QA question-answer pairs from image captions.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Existing VQA datasets contain strong language and answer-distribution biases that let models perform well using the question alone rather than image understanding. Bias also appears in yes/no imbalance, common question types, and phrasing cues.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Current VQA datasets are limited by small size, restricted scene diversity, clutter and difficult lighting in some datasets, biased question/answer distributions, sensitivity to question phrasing, and evaluation schemes that can be gamed or inflate scores. The paper also warns that multiple-choice evaluation can undermine true VQA by letting systems infer the answer from provided choices rather than actually answer the question.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper discusses positive social impact through accessibility for blind and visually impaired users, improved human-computer interaction, and image retrieval. It also notes that dataset bias limits deployment of current VQA systems.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The datasets are intended to train and evaluate VQA systems/algorithms and serve as benchmarks for assessing image understanding. The paper recommends using them carefully because current benchmarks are biased and insufficient to claim VQA is solved.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For COCO-QA, QA pairs were automatically generated from image captions using an NLP algorithm; longer sentences were broken into smaller chunks for processing.

description.evidence: Beginning in 2014, five major datasets for VQA have been publicly released. These datasets enable VQA systems to be trained and evaluated. As of this article, the main datasets for VQA are DAQUAR [30], COCO-QA [31], The VQA Dataset [32], FM-IQA [33], Visual7W [34], and Visual Genome [35].

datePublished.evidence: Beginning in 2014, five major datasets for VQA have been publicly released.

inLanguage.evidence: Visual Question Answering (VQA) is a computer vision task where a system is given a text-based question about an image, and it must infer the answer.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: “QA pairs based on images from the NYU-DepthV2 Dataset”; “QA pairs are created for images using an Natural Language Processing (NLP) algorithm that derives them from the COCO image captions”; “It contains human generated answers and questions”; “Two distinct modes of data collection were used to make the dataset. In the free-form method, annotators were free to ask any question about an image... prompting workers to ask questions about specific image regions”; “SHAPES consists of 244 unique questions, with every question asked about each of the 64 images in the dataset.”

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: “based on images from the NYU-DepthV2 Dataset”; “another dataset based on COCO”; “Visual Genome [35] consists of 108,249 images that occur in both YFCC100M [43] and COCO images.”

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: “based on images from the NYU-DepthV2 Dataset”; “derives them from the COCO image captions”; “another dataset based on COCO”; “consists of 108,249 images that occur in both YFCC100M [43] and COCO images”; “Region-specific question prompting was made possible using Visual Genome’s descriptive bounding-box annotations”; “consists of shapes of varying arrangements, types, and colors.”

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: “In COCO-QA [31], QA pairs are created for images using an Natural Language Processing (NLP) algorithm that derives them from the COCO image captions.”; “For The VQA Dataset, annotators generated ten answers per question.”; “The second metric is to rate an answer on a 3-point scale of totally wrong (0), partially correct (1), and perfectly correct (2).”

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: “Using AccuracyV QA, the inter-human agreement on COCO-VQA is only 83.3%.”; “Inter-human agreement is especially poor for ‘Why’ questions, with over 59% of these questions having less than three annotators giving exactly the same answer.”; “The dataset’s creators proposed two ways to use these answers, which they called average consensus and min consensus.”

rai:annotationsPerItem.evidence: “For DAQUAR-consensus, an average of five human annotated ground truth answers per question were collected.”; “For The VQA Dataset, annotators generated ten answers per question.”

rai:machineAnnotationTools.evidence: “In COCO-QA [31], QA pairs are created for images using an Natural Language Processing (NLP) algorithm that derives them from the COCO image captions.”

rai:dataBiases.evidence: The datasets tend to have strong bias. These two factors make language a much stronger prior than the image features alone.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: While DAQUAR was a pioneering dataset for VQA, it is too small to successfully train and evaluate more complex models.

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: The most immediate is as an aid to blind and visually impaired individuals, enabling them to get information about images both on the web and in the real world.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: These datasets enable VQA systems to be trained and evaluated.
